findings.title: Bulk delete has no ownership check (IDOR)
findings.description: delete_expenses_bulk() accepts user_id but never uses it to scope the DELETE. The query only filters by `id IN (...)`, so any authenticated user can pass arbitrary expense_ids belonging to other users and delete them. The WHERE clause must also include `AND user_id = ?` to prevent cross-account deletion.

findings.title: User row deleted before dependent rows
findings.description: delete_account() deletes from `users` first, then `expenses` and `tokens` that reference user_id. If foreign key constraints are enforced (PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON) this will raise an integrity error; if not enforced, an early failure/crash after the first statement still leaves expenses/tokens referencing a now-deleted user_id (orphaned rows), defeating the GDPR full-removal goal. Dependent rows should be deleted before the parent user row.

findings.title: Multi-statement deletion not wrapped in a transaction
findings.description: The three DELETE statements in delete_account() are executed independently with no transaction/commit-or-rollback boundary. If the process crashes or an exception occurs between statements (e.g. a locked table or FK violation), the account ends up partially deleted, leaving inconsistent state and, for a GDPR-motivated deletion, residual personal data.

findings.title: No tests for new deletion functions
findings.description: Neither delete_expenses_bulk() nor delete_account() has accompanying tests. Given these are destructive, security-sensitive operations, tests should at minimum cover: bulk delete of a mix of owned/unowned expense IDs (to catch the IDOR), empty expense_ids list, and full account deletion verifying expenses/tokens/user rows are all removed and behavior on partial failure.
